items.title: [Bug] [Portability][MSVC]: M_LOG2E is unavailable when building Flash Attention with NVCC and MSVC
items.body:
### Your current environment

### Environment

- Windows Server 2025
- Visual Studio Build Tools with MSVC
- CUDA/NVCC 13.2
- Python 3.12
- PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130
- SystemPanic/vllm-windows 0.25-based deployment
- DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731
- 4 x H200 NVL GPUs, SM90a

### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Background

I encountered this issue while building vllm-project/flash-attention through SystemPanic/vllm-windows for a deployment serving DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 on 4 x H200 NVL GPUs.

### Problem

Several Flash Attention CUDA source files use `M_LOG2E` in softmax and `exp2f` scale calculations:

    csrc/flash_attn/flash_api.cpp
    csrc/flash_attn/src/softmax.h
    hopper/flash_bwd_preprocess_kernel.h
    hopper/mainloop_fwd_sm80.hpp
    hopper/mainloop_fwd_sm90_tma_gmma_ws.hpp
    hopper/mainloop_bwd_sm80.hpp
    hopper/mainloop_bwd_sm90_tma_gmma_ws.hpp
    hopper/softmax.h

Examples include:

    params.scale_softmax_log2 =
        softmax_scale * M_LOG2E;

and:

    const float max_scaled =
        max(mi) == -INFINITY
            ? 0.f
            : max(mi) * (
                  Scale_max ? scale : float(M_LOG2E));

`M_LOG2E` represents `log2(e)` and is commonly available in GNU/Linux build environments. Its availability is implementation-specific, however, and MSVC normally exposes the `M_*` constants only when `_USE_MATH_DEFINES` is defined before the relevant math header is included.

I understand that native Windows may not be part of the supported build matrix. This appears to be a small source-portability issue rather than a request for broader Windows support.

### Tested workaround

The working downstream build replaces `M_LOG2E` with the corresponding float constant:

    - float(M_LOG2E)
    + 1.4426950408889634f

For example:

    - params.scale_softmax_log2 =
    -     softmax_scale * M_LOG2E;
    + params.scale_softmax_log2 =
    +     softmax_scale * 1.4426950408889634f;

The replacement preserves the intended `log2(e)` scale used by the float-based softmax and `exp2f` paths.

Applying the replacement to all affected occurrences allowed the Flash Attention extensions to build successfully with NVCC and MSVC.

### Related PyTorch-side solution

The discussion in: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54007

indicates that a PyTorch-side update may resolve this compatibility issue in the Windows build environment and perhaps could the same change be done here as well.

### Other possible solutions

The affected NVCC and MSVC targets could define:

    _USE_MATH_DEFINES=1

For example:

    target_compile_definitions(
        <target> PRIVATE _USE_MATH_DEFINES=1
    )

Alternatively, Flash Attention could use a project-owned `constexpr` value for `log2(e)` instead of depending on the host math-header configuration.

The source-level constant would be independent of PyTorch headers, build flags, and math-header include order.

### Repository context

Seven affected files are inherited from Dao-AILab/flash-attention.

The vllm-project fork additionally contains an affected occurrence in:

    hopper/softmax.h

I am reporting the complete set here because this is the Flash Attention fork built by vLLM.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: Hybrid mamba/attention page alignment inflates attention blocks to 7808 tokens — per-request KV footprint of ~23 giant pages collapses concurrency and prefix caching (GLM-5.3-Flash/Glm5Next)
items.body:
## Summary

On hybrid linear-attention models (GDN/mamba-class state + full attention —
here GLM-5.3-Flash "Glm5Next", same shape as Qwen3-Next), vLLM aligns the
attention block size upward so one attention page's bytes ≥ one mamba state
page's bytes:

```
INFO [interface.py:931] Setting attention block size to 7808 tokens to ensure
that attention page size is >= mamba page size.
```

With ~23 KV-cache groups (GDN state groups + attention groups + indexer +
spec-decode), each group needs at least one page per running request, so
**every request pins a fixed ~23-page footprint regardless of prompt
length** — measured 118k-150k token-equivalents per request on a 2x RTX PRO
6000 (SM120) TP2/DCP2 deployment. Consequences:

1. **Concurrency ceiling collapses.** With a 457,880-token pool
   (DFlash drafter config), a 12-token prompt occupies 32.9% of the pool;
   only 2-3 requests of ANY size run, the rest queue on capacity. We
   traced a production multi-agent collapse (aggregate decode 8-30 tok/s
   across 6 agents) to exactly this.
2. **Prefix caching becomes near-useless.** Each admission's giant
   allocation churns the free queue LRU and evicts cached hashes: a cached
   35k-token prompt is fully evicted after just 3 interleaved 35k
   admissions (hits 23,808 -> 0, TTFT 2.3s -> 7.1s). Hit granularity is
   also 7,808 tokens per block.
3. Capping `--max-model-len` does not help: the pool shrinks
   proportionally (measured 457,880 -> 234,194 tokens at 98304) and the
   23-page fixed footprint remains ~29-33% of pool.

## Measurements (GLM-5.3-Flash EXL3 4bpw, TP2 EP2 DCP2, SM120)

| Config | Pool (tokens) | Tiny-request footprint | Ceiling (tiny reqs) |
|---|---|---|---|
| DFlash drafter, ctx 303104 | 457,880 | 150.5k (32.9%) | 3 |
| DFlash drafter, ctx 98304 | 234,194 | 67.3k (28.8%) | 3 |
| MTP3, ctx 303104 | 1,279,772 | 118.6k (9.3%) | 8+ |

Usage gauge steps confirm the pool is only 70 / 80 / 248 pages
respectively, tiny requests taking exactly 23 pages in every config.

## Root cause

`vllm/platforms/interface.py` (`may_override_attention_block_size` area):

```python
attn_block_size = kernel_block_alignment_size * cdiv(
    mamba_page_size, kernel_block_alignment_size * attn_page_size_1_token)
...
if cache_config.block_size < attn_block_size:
    cache_config.block_size = attn_block_size
```

The code itself notes the constraint is relaxable:

```python
# TODO(tdoublep): this constraint can be relaxed fairly
# easily by changing the way we layout chunks in the
# mamba2 kernels.
```

## Ask

Allow one mamba state page to span multiple attention-sized pool pages
(virtual splitting — the same pattern some backends already use for
indexer storage blocks), or otherwise decouple attention block size from
mamba page size. Attention blocks back at 64-256 tokens would restore
normal admission granularity and prefix-cache utility for hybrid models;
the per-request GDN state cost itself is architectural and fine.

## Environment

- vLLM 0.1.dev20111+g7f1e92bec (community build, B12X lineage, image
  `verdictai/glm53-flash-exl3-k4:r19-sm120-tp2-ep2-dcp2-v84-language-only`)
- GLM-5.3-Flash EXL3 4bpw, `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4_ds_mla`,
  `--attention-backend B12X_MLA_SPARSE`, TP2 EP2 DCP2, chunked prefill
  2072, spec decode DFlash k4 / MTP3
- 2x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96GB (SM120), driver 595.84
- Repro scripts available (concurrency staircase + interleave cache-depth
  probe), happy to attach.

items.title: [Bug]: sampler warmup misses the plain-greedy path — spec-decode rejection kernels JIT on the first request
items.body:
Sibling of #54425 — same function, a second missing dimension. Filing separately because the
missing path and the observable failure are different; I have not touched that issue.

`SamplingParams.for_sampler_warmup()` is documented as "Set parameters to exercise all sampler
logic", but every warmup request gets `temperature=0.9`, so the warmup never takes the
`needs_logits_processing == False` early return in `Sampler.apply_sampling_params()` — the path
a plain `temperature=0` request uses.

With spec decoding that has a visible consequence. The startup warmup *does* reach
`rejection_sample()` (`_run_decode_step` populates `scheduled_spec_decode_tokens`), but it only
ever arrives there in fp32. dtype is a Triton compile key, so
`_compute_local_logits_stats_kernel`, `_rejection_kernel` and `_resample_kernel` are never
compiled for the model dtype and JIT on the first real greedy request:

```
startup (for_sampler_warmup) : needs_logits_processing=True  -> fp32
first temperature=0 request  : needs_logits_processing=False -> bfloat16   <- JIT here
```

`num_logits` is the same on both sides, so shape is held constant; warming the model dtype
alone takes the three `jit_monitor` warnings to zero. Measured first-request penalty on my box:
**+613 ms (52.1%)**. With `--jit-monitor-mode=error` the monitor is configured to raise on that
request (`vllm/utils/jit_monitor.py`), so this is not only a latency issue.

### The general shape (why this and #54425 are the same bug)

`warmup()` enumerates the **batch-shape** space carefully — `decode_steps`
(`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/warmup.py` L391-409 on main `@cacc429f6`) covers all-spec, mixed
spec/non-spec, single-request and no-draft-token variants, and L222-225 budgets for exactly
that (`num_decode_steps = 5 if num_spec_steps > 0 else 3`). But it samples the
**sampling-parameter** space at exactly one point — L280:

```python
sampling_params = SamplingParams.for_sampler_warmup()   # one object, all requests
```

#54425 is one axis of that point (no `seed` → FlashInfer is chosen, the seeded native
top-k/top-p + Gumbel path never runs). This report is another (`temperature=0.9` →
`needs_logits_processing` short-circuit never runs → the greedy dtype is never compiled).
Both are "the docstring says all sampler logic, and one dimension is pinned".

### Suggested fix

Same shape as #54425's: **run more than one sampler warmup configuration**, rather than
special-casing either axis. Concretely, either

1. add a second pass with a plain `SamplingParams()` (greedy) alongside the existing one, or
2. have `for_sampler_warmup()` return a small *list* of configurations and let `warmup()`
   iterate over it the way it already iterates over `decode_steps` (L409) — which would
   close #54425 and this one with the same change, and rides the structure already there.

I have a working local patch for the narrow greedy case (18 lines in
`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/warmup.py`) that takes the JIT warnings to zero, but it clears an internal
sampler buffer for the replay, which I don't think is the right shape to upstream. Happy to
send whichever of (1)/(2) you prefer as a PR.

### Environment

Intel XPU (Arc Pro B70), vLLM main `@cacc429f6` (2026-08-28), spec decode `qwen3_5_mtp`,
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MXFP4. I carry one unrelated local patch (an mxfp4 `register_fake`);
`sampling_params.py` and `warmup.py` are stock. No CUDA box here to confirm, and as far as I
can tell nothing in this path branches on platform, but I can't verify that claim on hardware.

Throughput decays continuously while the GPU goes idle, because the engine spends its time in single-threaded Python re-detokenizing every running sequence on every decode step. At real reasoning lengths this made the model about 11x slower than comparable 30B models on the same hardware. The mechanism is as follows. When a request has structured output and `--reasoning-parser muse_glimmer`, the engine calls `ReasoningParser.is_reasoning_end_streaming(all_token_ids, delta_ids)` every decode step to decide whether the grammar may start masking ([`vllm/v1/structured_output/__init__.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/structured_output/__init__.py), `should_advance`). The Muse-Glimmer implementation ignores `delta_ids` and re-detokenizes the entire sequence, then runs channel regexes over the decoded text: ```python def is_reasoning_end_streaming( self, input_ids: Sequence[int], delta_ids: Iterable[int] ) -> bool: return self.is_reasoning_end(list(input_ids)) # full decode, every step ``` Cost per generated token is therefore O(sequence length), i.e. quadratic per sequence, for every running request, inside EngineCore's step loop. Because of the correctness bug in the same predicate (#52594) it currently never fires on a no-tool turn, so it is polled until the end of the response, which makes the cost worst-case on `main`. For parsers of models that wrap reasoning in `...` tags this call is a token-id membership test. For muse_glimmer it is a full `tokenizer.decode()` plus a regex scan. ### Measured impact Muse-Glimmer-30B, concurrency 50, 16k reasoning budget, JSON schema requested: - throughput decays 260 to 170 tok/s as sequences grow (a continuous decay, not a plateau), with the GPU at about 150 W of its 300 W limit and `EngineCore` CPU pinned under one core - about 4.9 ms per decode step is spent inside this one predicate at those lengths, which is about 244 ms of serial Python per engine step at concurrency 50 Timing the predicate directly (CPU, best of 30, real Muse tokenizer): | prefix tokens | µs/call | | --- | --- | | 512 | 543 | | 2,048 | 2,224 | | 8,192 | 9,370 | | 16,384 | 19,526 | The cost is linear per call, and the call happens once per token per running request. ### Related work - #52594 reports the correctness half of the same predicate: it never fires on the `to=user` answer channel, so the schema is silently dropped. - #52390 and #53404 fix that correctness half. Neither changes the per-step cost, and the predicate still decodes the full sequence on every step. Once they make structured output usable for this model, more requests will exercise this path. - #52106 and #51133 fix a different quadratic, the budget-holder marker scan in [`thinking_budget_state.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/sample/thinking_budget_state.py). That is a different file and a different problem. ### Proposed fix The predicate can only flip False to True on a step whose delta completes a channel header, and every header ends with `<|message|>`. Collecting once per tokenizer the token ids that could supply that marker's final character (ids whose text starts with a non-empty suffix of `<|message|>` or contains it) gives an O(len(delta)) prefilter, because a step with no such id returns False without detokenizing anything. Fix PR: #54454 (draft, stacked on #52390). It works with the current parser and with #52390's rework, because the observation it relies on (a channel can only open by completing `<|message|>`) does not depend on what the full check answers.

items.title: [ROCm] DFlash unusable for GLM-5.3-Flash: glm5next lacks SupportsEagle3, and ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE has no non-causal path
items.body:
### DFlash on GLM-5.3-Flash / ROCm: the target model interface is missing, and the sparse-MLA backend cannot do non-causal

Trying to run `incoai/GLM-5.3-Flash-DFlash2` as a drafter for `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` on 8x MI350X (gfx950, ROCm 7.2.3, TP8), I hit two separate walls. The first has a small fix; the second looks structural.

**1. `models/glm5next/` does not implement `SupportsEagle3`.**

```
RuntimeError: Model does not support EAGLE3 interface
```

DFlash needs the target model to expose auxiliary hidden states from the layers named in the drafter's `target_layer_ids`. `glm5next` implements neither `EagleModelMixin` nor `SupportsEagle3`. Wiring it the way `qwen3_moe.py` does works — with one GLM-specific caveat worth recording:

```python
class Glm5NextModel(nn.Module, EagleModelMixin):
    ...
        # residual=None: on GLM-5.3 `residual` is the mHC bundle of several
        # residual streams, not a single same-shaped residual, so the mixin's
        # default `hidden_states + residual` does not apply.
        aux_hidden_states = self._maybe_add_hidden_state(
            [], self.start_layer, hidden_states, None
        )
        for aux_idx, layer in enumerate(self._active_layers, start=self.start_layer):
            hidden_states, residual, post, comb = layer(...)
            self._maybe_add_hidden_state(
                aux_hidden_states, aux_idx + 1, hidden_states, None
            )
```

Passing `residual` as the mixin expects fails with `The size of tensor a (8192) must match the size of tensor b (4)` because of the manifold-constrained hyper-connections. With `None` the mixin stores the hidden state directly, which is what the drafter consumes.

**Verified harmless when unused**: with this in place and no drafter configured, throughput and acceptance are unchanged (2 773 tok/s, acceptance 3.06 at 96 concurrency, within the ±5 % run-to-run spread) — `_maybe_add_hidden_state` is a no-op while `aux_hidden_state_layers` is empty.

**2. After that, the drafter loads and then the GPU aborts.**

```
DFlash2Qwen3ForCausalLM loaded (0.21 s)
:0:rocdevice.cpp:3586: Callback: Queue aborting with error :
HSA_STATUS_ERROR_EXCEPTION: An HSAIL operation resulted in a hardware exception. code: 0x1016
```

No Python traceback — a kernel faults. The cause looks like the non-causal requirement from #41559/#40632. `DFlashSpeculator` passes `use_non_causal=self.requires_non_causal`, but grepping for `causal` across the backends:

| backend | occurrences of `causal` |
|---|---|
| `flash_attn` | 51 |
| `triton_attn` | 5 |
| `mla/indexer` | 1 |
| **`mla/rocm_aiter_mla_sparse`** | **0** |

`ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE` — the only backend GLM-5.3-Flash can use on ROCm — has no notion of causality at all; it is causal-only by construction. The drafter's non-causal cross-attention then hands the kernel a shape it was not built for.

Things I ruled out along the way: it is not memory (`--gpu-memory-utilization 0.85` fails identically), not the fp8 KV cache (`--kv-cache-dtype bfloat16` fails identically, so #41559's bf16 restriction is not what is biting here), and not the `CandidateSelector`'s `@support_torch_compile` 4-D einsum (bypassing the decorator changes nothing).

#40632 was closed as "dflash is available now for both models functionally" for Kimi-K2.5 and Qwen3.5-27B — presumably on backends that do have a non-causal path. For sparse-MLA models on ROCm it does not appear to be reachable.

**Question:** is non-causal support in `ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE` on anyone's roadmap, or is DFlash structurally out of reach for GLM-5.3-Flash on AMD? Happy to send the `SupportsEagle3` wiring as a PR either way — it is useful on its own for any EAGLE3-family drafter, and it is measurably free when unused.

items.title: [RFC]: Weight version metadata in online RL: current behavior and open questions
items.body:
<!--### Motivation.-->

## Motivation

#48306 already covers weight-version metadata. The main open question is whether one value per request is enough when that request can continue through a weight update.

### A concrete case

```text
vLLM accepts request R while weight version v7 is active
  -> vLLM generates R's output tokens [0, 57) with v7
  -> the RL controller updates vLLM to weight version v8
  -> vLLM generates R's output tokens [57, 128) with v8
```

After R finishes, `/weight_info` returns v8 because it reports the engine's current weight-version label at query time. Draft #53199 would attach v7 to R because it records the weight version when vLLM accepts the request. Neither scalar shows that v7 generated tokens [0, 57) and v8 generated tokens [57, 128); token spans do. KV reuse across versions is a separate correctness issue covered by #48312.

A version-based freshness check also needs metadata when the system cannot tell which policy generated the data—for example, with queues, replay, async actors, partial or in-flight rollouts, or delayed and failed replica updates.

If the RL system stops new requests, waits for all running requests to finish, updates every rollout replica, confirms that all updates succeeded, resets the required caches, and only then resumes generation, the iteration ID is usually enough. Request- or token-level metadata may not be needed.

## Questions for vLLM

The current design leaves four questions:

1. Should vLLM return the weight version that generated an output, or only expose the weight version that is current when queried?
2. Must one request use only one weight version? If not, should its output list each token range and the weight version used for that range?
3. If one weight version is returned for a request, should vLLM record it when the request enters the engine, when it is first scheduled, or when its first output token is generated?
4. When does a new local weight version become active: after the weights finish loading, or only after related caches and runtime state are ready?

### Responsibilities

| Task | Meaning | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Weight update | Assign the global version and coordinate its installation | RL controller |
| Version record | Report which local version generated the output for a request or token range | Rollout engine |
| Freshness | Decide whether a sample is too old | RL buffer / controller |
| Policy mismatch | Measure and handle the difference between rollout and training policies | Trainer, using rollout logprobs |

Version lag and logprob ratios have different jobs:

| Signal | Definition | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Version lag | `current_trainer_version - sample_version` | Check age; keep, drop, or regenerate data |
| Logprob ratio | `exp(train_logprob_t - rollout_logprob_t)` | Correct off-policy data for the same token and context |

For a sample with several weight versions, the oldest version gives a conservative age check. Version lag does not say how much the policy changed. Loss masks can exclude selected tokens.

### Current frameworks

| System | Current pattern |
| --- | --- |
| **vLLM** | #49040 stores a caller-provided label in `EngineCore`. `/weight_info` returns the current label. Draft #53199 records it at request admission. |
| **SGLang** | Main returns controller-provided versions as output-token spans, so one request can contain several versions. SGLang pull request 35926 added this support. |
| **VERL** | The controller tracks `global_steps` and uses update barriers. Rollout logprobs handle policy mismatch. |
| **Slime** | The trainer sends a version counter with updates and records one version per generation. Correction uses rollout logprobs and loss masks. |
| **Miles** | Numeric versions filter stale async samples. Main keeps one version per generation call; Miles pull request 1891 proposes token spans. |

For the request above, a native SGLang `/generate` response contains:

```json
{
  "meta_info": {
    "weight_version": "v8",
    "weight_versions": [
      {"version": "v7", "start": 0, "end": 57},
      {"version": "v8", "start": 57, "end": 128}
    ]
  }
}
```

Each `[start, end)` range uses indexes into the generated output tokens; prompt tokens are not included. `weight_version` is the version in the last visible span.

### Frontier model technical reports

Public reports mainly answer two questions: “Is this data too old?” and “How should training use it if it is kept?” They may omit internal production details, so the text below only covers what is public.

- **[GLM-5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15763):** GLM-5 gives the clearest public example of version-based freshness. Because rollout and training run at the same time, one response may cross several weight updates. The RL system records `[w0, ..., wk]` for each response and drops it when `current_version - w0 > τ`. The report uses this list for an oldest-version freshness check. For correction, rollout logprobs are used to mask tokens when the train-rollout ratio is too low or too high. The report does not map the versions to token ranges.

- **[GLM-5.2 / SAO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07508):** In SAO, each trajectory becomes available for training as soon as it finishes; the algorithm does not wait for a GRPO-style group. This reduces delay, but one long trajectory may still cross several rollout-model versions. SAO uses the same rollout-logprob ratio and token mask for correction, but it does not publish a weight-version field or a version-lag cutoff.

- **DeepSeek:** [V3.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02556) does not publish a version counter. It says rollout data becomes off-policy when one rollout batch is split into minibatches and used across several gradient updates, and when inference and training engines differ. The inference engine returns sampling probabilities; training masks highly mismatched responses with negative advantage and reuses the rollout's MoE expert routes and top-p/top-k masks. [V4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348) logs every generated token and saves KV state so interrupted requests can resume. The report presents this as fault recovery, not as a freshness mechanism, and neither report publishes a weight-version format.

- **Qwen:** [GSPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18071) corrects off-policy data at the response level: token logprob differences are combined into one length-normalized sequence ratio, and the whole response is clipped using that value. The paper says this is more tolerant of small train-inference numerical differences and can use likelihoods returned by the inference engine. The [Qwen3.5 release blog](https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3.5) says its asynchronous system bounds gradient staleness and uses rollout router replay and multi-turn rollout locking, but it does not define those rules or publish a weight-version format.

- **Kimi:** [K2.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02276) runs agent tasks as asynchronous coroutines. Here, this means concurrent task execution; the report does not say that weights update asynchronously. It keeps exact rollout token IDs and logprobs, then masks tokens whose train-rollout log-ratio is too large. [K3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24653) gives a clear partial-rollout flow: training starts after enough trajectories finish, while unfinished trajectories are queued and resumed in the next iteration. One trajectory can therefore cross several iterations and become stale; K3 uses per-token regularization to handle it. Neither report publishes weight-version tags.

When exposed, version lag can reject old data; logprobs, replay data, and masks handle the data that is kept. Among these reports, only GLM-5 clearly publishes a response-level weight-version list, and none defines a token-range response schema like SGLang's.
