It excludes weights, caches, compiled modules, images, credentials, private networking, full service logs, and any host-control/rollback code.

I can run one maintainer-specified near-stock build or bounded diagnostic on the same two-GB10 cluster, provided the requested commit set and instrumentation are explicit. I would prefer not to repeat the unchanged startup because the first run faulted both GPUs.

items.title: First boot of a new `(max-num-batched-tokens, max-num-seqs)` shape is granted a ~5% smaller KV cache than subsequent identical boots
items.body:
### Environment

- vLLM 0.28.0, V1 engine, TP=2
- 2 × NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24,564 MiB each), driver 580.173.02, CUDA 13.0
- Qwen/Qwen3-32B-AWQ, `--max-model-len 8192`
- Ubuntu 24.04, Python 3.12.3, `VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0`, `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True`

### Summary

Booting the server twice with byte-identical arguments gives two different `GPU KV cache size` values when the first boot is that shape's first ever. The second boot is granted roughly 5% more KV. The difference persists as long as the compile cache does, so a deployment's capacity depends on whether the cache happened to be warm when it started.

### Reproduction

Pick a `(--max-num-batched-tokens, --max-num-seqs)` pair this machine has never served, and boot it twice, waiting for GPU memory to return to idle in between so residual memory is not a factor:

```bash
drain() {  # wait for VRAM to return to idle before starting
  while [ "$(nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used --format=csv,noheader,nounits \
            | paste -sd+ | bc)" -ge 450 ]; do sleep 2; done
}

for i in 1 2; do
  drain
  vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-32B-AWQ --port 8000 --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
    --max-model-len 8192 --max-num-batched-tokens 1536 --max-num-seqs 48 \
    --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --enable-prefix-caching &
  # wait for /health, then grep the log:
  #   grep -o 'GPU KV cache size: [0-9,]* tokens' server.log
  # ...then shut down
done
```

### Observed

Two independently chosen novel shapes, strict drain to 255 MiB before **both** boots:

| shape (mbt/mns) | boot 1 (first ever) | boot 2 (identical args) | difference | boot-1 startup | boot-2 startup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1536/48 | 82,688 tokens | 88,096 tokens | **+5,408** | 65s | 30s |
| 3072/96 | 82,256 tokens | 86,528 tokens | **+4,272** | 71s | 40s |

The first boot is also ~30–35 s slower to reach `/health` — the compile and CUDA-graph capture that the second boot loads from `~/.cache/vllm/torch_compile_cache`.

### Why it matters

The KV pool is the main capacity parameter of a deployment, and this makes it depend on cache state rather than on the arguments. On this box the effect (~5,408 tokens) is **larger than the difference between `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.82` and `0.85`** (5,776 tokens), so two runs of the same configuration can straddle what was meant to be a deliberate configuration change. It is silent: the server starts normally and reports its pool as though the arguments determined it. Anyone A/B testing server configurations, or sizing capacity from a first deployment, inherits an uncontrolled ~5% term.

### Workaround

Boot each new shape once to populate the compile cache and discard that run, then measure. Waiting for VRAM to drain is *not* sufficient on its own — see below.

### What was ruled out

- **Residual GPU memory.** 10 boots alternating a strict drain (<450 MiB) with vLLM's default (<1500 MiB) gave 87,200 tokens every time. Forcing the issue with SIGKILL and a 1–3 s restart gave 87,200 every time as well; the driver had already reclaimed everything and pre-boot VRAM read 255 MiB in all 14 boots.
- **Utilisation, batched-token and sequence budgets** are held constant across each pair above.


### Reproduction data

All raw data is public:

- **[results/BOOT_MATRIX.md](https://github.com/vitalyrodnenko/replay-sim/blob/main/results/BOOT_MATRIX.md)** — the full write-up: the
  10-boot drain matrix, the SIGKILL extension, and the novel-shape test that reproduces
  the effect.
- **[results/boot_matrix_novel.csv](https://github.com/vitalyrodnenko/replay-sim/blob/main/results/boot_matrix_novel.csv)** and
  **[boot_matrix_novel2.csv](https://github.com/vitalyrodnenko/replay-sim/blob/main/results/boot_matrix_novel2.csv)** — the two
  reproducing pairs (shape 1536/48 and 3072/96), pre-boot VRAM and granted pool per boot.
- **[results/boot_matrix.csv](https://github.com/vitalyrodnenko/replay-sim/blob/main/results/boot_matrix.csv)** — the 10 alternating-drain
  boots that came back identical, ruling the drain threshold out.
- **[results/boot_matrix_hostile.csv](https://github.com/vitalyrodnenko/replay-sim/blob/main/results/boot_matrix_hostile.csv)** — SIGKILL
  plus 1-3 s restart, also identical.
- Server startup logs for every boot above:
  [novelshape_1](https://github.com/vitalyrodnenko/replay-sim/blob/main/results/logs/novelshape_1.log),
  [novelshape_2](https://github.com/vitalyrodnenko/replay-sim/blob/main/results/logs/novelshape_2.log),
  [novelshape2_1](https://github.com/vitalyrodnenko/replay-sim/blob/main/results/logs/novelshape2_1.log),
  [novelshape2_2](https://github.com/vitalyrodnenko/replay-sim/blob/main/results/logs/novelshape2_2.log),
  and `bootmatrix_1..10.log` in the same directory. Each contains the
  `GPU KV cache size:` line quoted above and the full engine config.

### Caveats

- Single machine, single model, TP=2 only; not reproduced on other hardware.
- Two points from earlier work on this box do not fit a pure first-boot-compilation story: one shape's first boot came in high, and one repeat boot came in low. The effect reproduces on demand but is not fully characterised.
- The exact allocation being counted was not instrumented; the association with startup time is strong but indirect.

---
*Filed from a reproducible benchmark harness; the full run record, including every raw log referenced above, is at https://github.com/vitalyrodnenko/replay-sim*

items.title: [Model] Cohere Transcribe fails to initialize on Turing (fp16): expected scalar type Float but found Half in RelPositionMultiHeadAttention
items.body:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

Serving `CohereLabs/cohere-transcribe-03-2026` with `--dtype float16` (required on Turing-class GPUs, which have no bf16 support) fails during engine initialization with:

```
RuntimeError: expected scalar type Float but found Half
```

in `RelPositionMultiHeadAttention.forward()` at `vllm/model_executor/models/cohere_asr.py` line 1183:

```python
matrix_bd = torch.matmul(q_with_bias_v, p.transpose(-2, -1))
```

Full traceback ends with `Engine core initialization failed. See root cause above. Failed core proc(s): {}` — the server never comes up.

### Root cause analysis

The relative-position bias parameters are created as fp32 and never participate in the model-wide dtype conversion:

```python
self.pos_bias_u = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(self.h, self.d_k), requires_grad=False)
self.pos_bias_v = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(self.h, self.d_k), requires_grad=False)
```

On a bf16-capable GPU, vLLM's model cast (`model.to(dtype)`) covers these parameters. On Turing, vLLM logs `Casting torch.bfloat16 to torch.float16` and the activations become fp16, but `pos_bias_u/v` remain fp32 (the load path does not appear to convert them). The forward then computes `q_with_bias_v = (q + self.pos_bias_v)` — fp16 + fp32 promotes to fp32 — and the subsequent `torch.matmul(fp32, fp16)` raises. The failure occurs during the engine-init forward pass, before any request can be served.

I confirmed the identical code exists on `main` (verified 2026-08-29), so this affects current releases as well.

### Minimal fix (verified working)

```python
q_with_bias_u = (q + self.pos_bias_u.to(q.dtype)).transpose(1, 2)
q_with_bias_v = (q + self.pos_bias_v.to(q.dtype)).transpose(1, 2)
```

Applied as a mounted file override, the server initializes and transcribes correctly (WAV and Opus, multipart upload). Happy to open a PR with this change if maintainers confirm the approach.

## Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the troubleshooting guide
- [x] I tried to reproduce my issue with the latest version of vLLM (not a version from source)
- [x] The issue is not a question/discussion (use GitHub Discussions for that)

## Your current environment

- vLLM version: v0.28.0 (Docker image `vllm/vllm-openai:latest`, digest `61fc8a89…`; same code present on `main`)
- GPU: NVIDIA RTX 2060 6GB (Turing, compute capability 7.5)
- CUDA driver: 595.84; host Ubuntu 24.04 (Linux 7.0.0-28-generic); container runtime: nvidia
- Python 3.12 in image; PyTorch as shipped with the image

### Reproduction

```
docker run --runtime nvidia -p 8001:8001 \
  -v /path/to/cohere-transcribe-03-2026:/models/cohere:ro \
  vllm/vllm-openai:latest \
  /models/cohere --dtype float16 --max-model-len 1024 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --trust-remote-code --port 8001
```

Observed log excerpt:

```
WARNING ... Casting torch.bfloat16 to torch.float16.
...
RuntimeError: expected scalar type Float but found Half
  File ".../vllm/model_executor/models/cohere_asr.py", line 1183, in forward
    matrix_bd = torch.matmul(q_with_bias_v, p.transpose(-2, -1))
```

Related but distinct: open HF discussion on the model repo reports a segfault on A100 (bf16 path) with vLLM nightly — https://huggingface.co/CohereLabs/cohere-transcribe-03-2026/discussions/20 — possibly the same code region misbehaving on the other dtype path.

items.title: [ROCm] Fused shared experts unavailable for GLM-5.3-Flash: Fp8Config not handled by the FSE gate, and glm5next never wires it
items.body:
### Summary

GLM-5.3-Flash has `n_shared_experts = 1`, but AITER fused shared experts (FSE) cannot be used with it for two independent reasons. The first is a one-line gate I have a working patch for; the second is model wiring that needs an MTP-aware decision.

### 1. `Fp8Config` is not handled by the FSE compatibility gate

`is_shared_expert_quant_fse_compatible` (`model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/config_utils.py`) special-cases `DeepseekV4FP8Config` and `QuarkConfig`, then falls through to:

```
shared-expert FSE quantization compatibility is not implemented for Fp8Config
```

For a plain fp8 checkpoint this looks safe to allow. `Fp8Config` applies one global `weight_block_size` and one activation scheme to everything it covers, so the routed and shared experts carry the same scheme by construction — the only way they can diverge is if exactly one side sits in `ignored_layers`. GLM-5.3-Flash-FP8 has `weight_block_size: [128, 128]`, `activation_scheme: dynamic`, `ignored_layers: null`.

```python
    from vllm.model_executor.layers.quantization.fp8 import Fp8Config

    if isinstance(quant_config, Fp8Config):
        from vllm.model_executor.layers.quantization.utils.quant_utils import (
            is_layer_skipped,
        )

        ignored = quant_config.ignored_layers or []
        experts_skipped = is_layer_skipped(expert_prefix, ignored, match_mode="suffix")
        shared_skipped = is_layer_skipped(
            shared_expert_prefix, ignored, match_mode="suffix"
        )
        if experts_skipped != shared_skipped:
            side = shared_expert_prefix if shared_skipped else expert_prefix
            return False, (
                f"fp8 quantization covers only one side of the fusion ({side} "
                "is in ignored_layers)"
            )
        return True, None
```

With this the gate opens and the warning disappears. Happy to send it as a PR on its own if you want it independent of the rest.

### 2. `models/glm5next/` does not wire FSE at all

`Glm5NextMoE` passes `shared_experts=<module>` to `FusedMoEFactory` but neither `n_shared_experts` nor `fuse_shared_experts`, so the shared expert always runs as a separate module over every token. Wiring it the way `glm4_moe.py` does is mechanical — construction flag via `resolve_layer_fused_shared_expert`, `maybe_fuse_shared_experts` in `load_weights`, `num_experts + n_shared` in the expert params mapping. I did that and the model loads and answers correctly (needle found at 6.7k and 110k tokens).

**Where it stops:** the MTP block. `model.layers.45.mtp_block.mlp` is also a `Glm5NextMoE`, so it gets the same construction-time fusion decision, but its checkpoint weights are named `model.layers.45.mtp_block.mlp.shared_experts.*` and `maybe_fuse_shared_experts` matches on the `mlp.shared_experts.` substring, so it catches the MTP block too. Excluding the MTP weights from the transform then leaves its dropped `shared_experts` module without a target:

```
KeyError: 'model.layers.45.mtp_block.mlp.shared_experts.down_proj.weight'
```

Gating the construction-time decision on `".mtp_block." not in prefix` did not resolve it either, so the module prefix seen at construction apparently does not carry the `mtp_block` component that the checkpoint name has. Keeping the two decisions in sync needs someone who knows how `Glm5NextMTP` is meant to share `Glm5NextMoE` — hence this issue rather than a PR.

`glm4_moe.py` sidesteps this with `skip_spec_layers(weights, self.config)` before the fuse transform; `models/glm5next/` has no equivalent.

### Is it worth it?

Unproven — I could not get to a clean A/B because of (2). The shared expert runs over *every* token as a separate GEMM (`moe_intermediate_size = 2048`, hidden 4096), so at decode-sized batches the saved launch plus the merged pass looks worthwhile, but I have no number to offer.

Context: 8x MI350X (gfx950), ROCm 7.2.3, TP8, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, tuned fMoE, indexer fix from #54359. Related: #54369.

items.title: [Perf][ROCm] Sparse-MLA/kpool backends fall back to rebuilding attention metadata per draft step, capping useful MTP depth at k=4
items.body:
### Summary

On ROCm with GLM-5.3-Flash, vLLM logs at startup:

```
Fused multi-step draft decode is not supported by attention backend(s)
DEEPSEEK_V32_INDEXER, KPOOL_TAIL, ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE;
falling back to rebuilding attention metadata between draft steps.
```

Because the metadata is rebuilt between every draft step, the per-step cost of MTP speculation is high enough that deeper speculation stops paying for itself well before the draft quality runs out. Measurements below quantify the gap.

### Measurements

8x MI350X (gfx950), ROCm 7.2.3, TP8, GLM-5.3-Flash-FP8, `--max-model-len 1048576`, 2 000-token context, 256 output tokens, unique per-request prefixes (nothing hits the prefix cache), warmup round then median of 3-4 rounds.

| `num_speculative_tokens` | acceptance length | draft acceptance rate | 1 user | 16 users | 64 users |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 2.57 | 78.4 % | 155 tok/s | 1 432 | 3 012 |
| **4** | **3.36** | 58.9 % | **173** | **1 499** | **3 055** |
| 6 | 3.76 | 46.0 % | 175 | 1 367 | 2 874 |

The accepted length keeps climbing (2.57 → 3.36 → 3.76), i.e. the draft head still has useful signal at k=6. But throughput peaks at k=4 and *falls* at k=6, which is what you would expect when each additional draft step carries a fixed metadata-rebuild cost rather than being fused.

Note this model has `num_nextn_predict_layers = 1`, so every draft token is another autoregressive pass through the same MTP head — the per-step overhead is paid k times.

### Why this matters

For latency-sensitive single-stream use, speculation is the main lever (at high concurrency the GPU is compute-saturated and speculation contributes almost nothing — see the 64-user column). Being capped at k=4 by framework overhead rather than by draft quality leaves measurable throughput on the table.

### Ask

Is fused multi-step draft decode feasible for these backends (`ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE`, `DEEPSEEK_V32_INDEXER`, `KPOOL_TAIL`), or is there a structural reason the sparse-indexer metadata cannot be built once for all draft steps? If it is mainly a matter of hoisting the metadata build, I am happy to test a patch on this hardware — I have the harness and the baseline numbers above.

Related: #54359 (a correctness bug in the same kpool indexer path on ROCm), #53906 (GLM-5.3-Flash support).

items.body:
### Motivation.

The filesystem secondary tier (`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/fs/`) is a data path with no integrity verification and no bound on how long a single I/O operation may take. #49328 established the partial-keep contract this builds on: a failed load marks its own cached lookup verdict a miss and reports how many blocks loaded before the failure, so earlier blocks survive. Two gaps remain on top of that:

1. **No data integrity verification.** Block contents written to the filesystem tier are never checksummed. `_load_block` detects a file shorter than `block_size` and deletes it, so truncation is caught. What is not caught is content that is the right length and the wrong bytes: bit rot on the storage device, a partially rewritten file, or a block written by an instance whose layout differs in a way the `FileMapper` path hash does not capture. Such a block is copied into the primary tier and consumed as attention KV, producing wrong logits with no error signal anywhere in the system.

2. **No deadline on filesystem I/O.** `batch_store_block` and `batch_load_block` run as a single pool task per job with no deadline. A stalled NFS mount, hung FUSE filesystem, or a device in error recovery blocks that pool thread indefinitely. The pool is bounded at `n_read_threads` + `n_write_threads` (16 + 16 by default), and read-priority threads fall back to the store queue and vice versa, so ~32 stuck operations stall all tiering traffic in both directions. This is the tier-side half of the problem reported in #49829: that issue bounds how long the scheduler waits on a `HIT_PENDING` block, but nothing bounds the write it is waiting for.

Two smaller gaps follow from the same code path:

1. **Stale temporary files are never reclaimed.** `_store_block` writes to `<dest>_<random>.tmp` and `os.replace` it, cleaning up the temp file if the write raises. If the engine dies between the two (OOM kill, SIGKILL, node preemption), the temp file survives with nothing that will ever remove it. On a long-lived shared PVC these accumulate without bound.

2. **No errno-based error classification.** Both the C and Python I/O paths already surface `errno` (`PyErr_SetFromErrnoWithFilename` in `csrc/fs_io.cpp`), and partial progress is already reported (`exc.num_succeeded` -> `JobResult.successful_keys`, added in #49328). Nothing consumes the errno. A transient `ESTALE` on an NFS remount is treated identically to a permanent `ENOSPC`: the remaining keys in the batch are marked a miss and recomputed.

These matter most on shared or network filesystems (NFS, POSIX PVCs), which the tier explicitly supports: `FileSystemTierManager` documents cross-instance cache sharing over a common `root_dir`.

### Proposed Change.

Four changes, each independently. Every one of them touches both I/O implementations: `vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/fs/io.py` is a pure-Python fallback, and `csrc/fs_io.cpp` (built as `vllm.fs_io_C`) is the path actually taken whenever the extension imports. 

### 1. Block-level checksum validation
**What:** Compute a CRC32C over each block when storing it to the filesystem tier, persist it with the block, and verify it on load. A mismatch deletes the file and marks the key a miss rather than returning corrupt KV.
**Design:**
- **Placement, given O_DIRECT.** The tier prefers `O_DIRECT` and falls back to buffered I/O only where the probe fails, so block payloads must stay length- and offset-aligned. A 4-byte trailer appended to the payload breaks that alignment for every block. Two viable options, and choosing between them is the main open question for this item:
  - *Padded trailer:* store the checksum in a full logical block appended after the payload, keeping the payload aligned. Costs one extra device block (512 B or 4 KiB) per file, where a file holds `blocks_per_chunk` blocks. This overhead is the main argument for the sidecar.
  - *Sidecar directory:* keep checksums in a separate file keyed by the same hash. Preserves the payload byte-for-byte, but loses the single-rename atomicity that `os.replace` gives today.
- **Verification point.** `_load_block` reads via `os.readv` directly into the primary tier's memoryview slice, so a block cannot be verified before it lands there. Verification happens after the read and before the key is reported as a successful load, and a mismatch is reported through the existing `num_succeeded` partial-keep path so preceding blocks in the batch are still kept.
- **On-disk format versioning.** `FileMapper._compute_base_path` derives the storage directory from a SHA-256 of `FileMapper.fields`. Enabling checksums changes the on-disk format, so it must add a field there. Without it, a cache directory written before the upgrade is read as if it carried checksums, and every block fails verification. This is a one-line change and the reason the item touches `file_mapper.py`.
- **Algorithm.** CRC32C is hardware-accelerated on x86 (SSE 4.2) and ARM (CRC extension) and is straightforward to implement in `csrc/fs_io.cpp` alongside the existing I/O, which avoids adding a Python dependency for the fast path.
- **Config:** `checksum_blocks: bool = False` as a `FileSystemTierManager` kwarg, plumbed through the tier config dict that `SecondaryTierFactory.create_secondary_tier` splats into the constructor. Defaulting to off keeps the change inert until the storage-overhead and throughput numbers are on the table.
- **Metric:** `vllm:kv_offload_tiering_checksum_failures`, labeled by tier. Existing counters in this subsystem are unsuffixed (`..._cascade_job_failures`, `..._promotion_job_failures`); `vllm:kv_offload_cpu_evictions_total` is the sole `_total` user, so this follows the local majority.

### 2. I/O deadline for filesystem jobs
**What:** Give each enqueued filesystem job a deadline. When it expires, report the job as failed to the tiering manager so the scheduler stops waiting, and account for the fact that the worker thread may still be blocked.
**Design:**
- Add a monotonic deadline to `JobState` at enqueue time. A periodic check in `DualQueueThreadPool.get_finished()` (the pool's own method; the tier-level API is `get_finished_jobs()`) publishes expired jobs to `_finished_q`.
- **Reconciling a reaped job is the core problem, not the timer.** `JobState.task_done` publishes a job when `_completed == _n_tasks` and decrements `_inflight_jobs` there. If the reaper publishes a job and its stuck task later completes, the job is published twice and `_inflight_jobs` goes negative, which breaks the `wait_idle()` that `drain_jobs()` and `shutdown()` depend on. The proposal is a terminal flag on `JobState`: the first publisher wins, the second is dropped, and `_inflight_jobs` is decremented exactly once. Reviewers should push on this part first.
- **Interrupting the I/O.** A blocked `os.write`/`os.readv` cannot be interrupted from Python, and the C path releases the GIL for the entire batch with no cancellation check, so a flag polled between blocks only works if `csrc/fs_io.cpp` grows one. Even then it cannot preempt a syscall already blocked in the kernel. The honest scope is: the deadline unblocks the *scheduler* promptly; the thread stays stuck until the filesystem returns. `p2p/manager.py::_reap_unbound_stores` is the in-tree precedent for this shape.
- **Config:** `io_timeout_seconds: float | None = None` (off by default) as a `FileSystemTierManager` kwarg.
- **Metric:** `vllm:kv_offload_tiering_io_timeouts`, labeled by tier and direction.

### 3. Stale temporary file cleanup
**What:** Reclaim `*.tmp` files left behind by a crashed engine.
**Design:**
- **A blind sweep at startup is not safe.** `FileSystemTierManager` documents cross-process cache sharing over a common `root_dir`, and `FileMapper` is constructed with `parallel_agnostic=True`, which forces `rank` to 0 for qualifying models. Multiple live instances therefore write into the same directory. Deleting every `*.tmp` at init would delete another running instance's in-flight temp files. The temp suffix is `_<random>.tmp` with no owner encoded, so ownership cannot be recovered from the name.
- Proposal: delete only temp files whose mtime is older than a conservative threshold (default 1 hour), which no in-flight write can plausibly reach. The `.o_direct_probe_<random>.tmp` files from `probe_o_direct` are covered by the same rule.
- Alternative worth discussing: encode the writing instance's identity in the temp suffix so a sweep can skip files belonging to a live PID. More precise, but does not help across containers or nodes, which is the deployment this tier targets.
- **Config:** `cleanup_stale_tmp_after_seconds: float | None = 3600.0`.

### 4. Transient error classification and retry
**What:** Use the `errno` already surfaced by both I/O paths to distinguish retryable from terminal failures, and retry the retryable ones once or twice before falling back to the existing partial-keep path.
**Design:**
- Classify: `EAGAIN`, `EIO`, `ESTALE`, `ETIMEDOUT`, `EINTR` retryable; `ENOSPC`, `EPERM`, `EACCES`, `ENOENT` terminal. `ENOENT` on load is an ordinary miss, not an error, and must not be retried. The open PR #52838 takes the same shape one layer up, dropping a failed store but escalating a failed load, and is worth keeping consistent with.
- Retry the failing block only, not the batch. `exc.num_succeeded` already identifies where the batch stopped, so a retry resumes there.
- Bound retries so they cannot extend a job past the item 2 deadline; a retry budget without a deadline reintroduces the unbounded wait this RFC is trying to remove. This is why this item lands last.
- **Metric:** `vllm:kv_offload_tiering_io_retries`, labeled by tier, direction, and errno.

### Out of scope: tracked in other threads
The following are deliberately excluded so this RFC does not duplicate or pre-empt work already under discussion. All are open issues rather than merged or in-flight changes, so none of the four items above depends on any of them landing.
- **Tier health tracking and circuit breaking.** Two RFCs already build per-tier gating: #50031 detects saturation from an EMA of store completion rate and drops cascade stores; #51240 defines a `TieringAdmissionPolicy` ABC and ships `CascadeBackpressurePolicy`, detecting saturation from an EMA of submission-to-completion latency and rejecting jobs in `should_admit`. #53485 exists to reconcile the two and argues #51240's hook is the integration point, since it is already wired into `create_store_job()`. An error-rate breaker is a different *signal* — a tier failing fast with `EIO` is not saturated, and neither EMA would trip — but it is the same *decision*, and `TieringAdmissionPolicy.on_completed(job, result)` already receives `JobResult.success`. It therefore belongs as a policy implementation under #51240 once that lands, not as a separate `health.py` and not as a section of this RFC. Metrics from items 1, 2, and 4 are what such a policy would act on.
- **Bounding how long the scheduler waits on an in-flight write.** #49829: `TieringOffloadingManager.lookup()` returns `HIT_PENDING` with no deadline and the scheduler re-polls in a hot loop, so a stalled write defers requests until the client timeout. Item 2 bounds the write itself. The two are complementary and neither subsumes the other.
- **Reclaiming leaked shared-memory segments after a crash.** #54002: `SharedOffloadRegion` never unlinks `/dev/shm/vllm_offload_<engine_id>.mmap`, and on Kubernetes `/dev/shm` survives container restarts, so a crash wedges the pod in CrashLoopBackOff. Same failure class as item 3 (an artifact outliving the process that made it) but a different artifact, a different owner, and a much sharper impact.
- **Recovering primary-tier ref-counts after a crash.** Not needed, and worth stating so reviewers do not ask. `CPUPrimaryTierOffloadingManager` inherits its block index and `ref_cnt` bookkeeping from `CPUOffloadingManager`, built in memory in `__init__` with no restore-from-disk path, and `SharedOffloadRegion` keys its backing file on `engine_id`, so a restarted engine gets a fresh region rather than reattaching to the old one. In-flight transfer state is therefore gone, not stale. The old region itself does leak, but that is the memory-reclamation problem in #54002, not a ref-count problem.

### Summary table
items are numbered in the order they should be merged, and the motivation list above uses the same numbering.
| Item | Needs a `csrc/fs_io.cpp` change | Priority |
|------|-------------------------------|----------|
| 1. Checksum validation | Yes | High — silent corruption has no error signal today |
| 2. I/O deadline | Yes, for a cancellation point | High — pool starvation stalls both directions |
| 3. Stale tmp cleanup | No | Medium — unbounded growth on shared PVCs |
| 4. Transient retry | Yes | Low — needs item 2's deadline to bound the retry budget |

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@varun-sundar-rabindranath 

### Any Other Things.

- Scope is the filesystem tier only. The P2P tier already has abort-on-timeout, abort-ack timeout, and `_reap_unbound_stores` in `p2p/manager.py`. The object store tier (`tiering/obj/`) would benefit from items 1 and 4 but is left out to keep each PR reviewable.
- Item 1 changes the on-disk format. Existing caches are not migrated: the `FileMapper` field change moves checksummed caches to a new directory, and operators enabling the flag start with a cold tier.
- Each PR adds unit tests for both the C and Python I/O paths. The existing `tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_fs_tier.py` covers both and is the pattern to follow. Fault injection for items 2 and 4 needs a stub that blocks or returns a chosen errno, since a real stalled mount is not reproducible in CI.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: Speculative decoding (mtp and dflash) silently disables prefix-cache hits for hybrid GDN models on nightly; worked on v0.24.0
items.body:
(analysis by Fable 5)
### Your current environment

- DGX Spark (GB10, `sm_121`/`sm_121a`, aarch64, 128 GB unified memory), Docker `--network host --gpus all --ipc host`
- Image: `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` → reports `v0.28.1rc1.dev43+g6f7df92a8`
- Comparison baseline on the same host: `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.24.0`
- Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` (hybrid GDN: 48 linear-attention + 16 full-attention layers, built-in MTP head). Also reproduced with `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` + `incoai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` (rev `dedf8df`).
- `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, `--max-model-len 65536`, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.30`, env `CUTE_DSL_ARCH=sm_121a`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On the current nightly, enabling **any** speculative decoding method (built-in `mtp` or `dflash`) on a hybrid GDN model silently drops `vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total` to **0** — align-mode prefix caching engages at startup (log: `Mamba cache mode is set to 'align' for Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`) but never hits, and repeated long prompts pay full re-prefill. The identical command minus `--speculative-config` hits normally. No crash, no warning — the caching is just inert, so this is easy to miss in production.

A/B on the same host, same model, same 18,219-token prompt sent twice (`max_tokens=10`):

| nightly config | TTFT req1 → req2 | `prefix_cache_hits_total` delta |
|---|---|---|
| APC only (no spec) | 9.46 s → **0.64 s** | **17,248** |
| APC + `{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}` | 23.6 s → 13.9 s* | **0** |
| APC + `{"method":"dflash", ..., "num_speculative_tokens":7}` | 12.9 s → 12.5 s | **0** |

\* the MTP row also shows a large decode regression on this platform (10.5 tok/s vs 19.7 on v0.24.0 with the same flags — possibly a separate sm_121 issue; noting it for context, not the subject of this report).

**On `v0.24.0`, MTP + align-mode APC coexist correctly** on the same host/model: repeated 9,901-token prompt → 8,000 tokens hit, TTFT 7.27 s → 1.33 s, with `mtp` k=3 active. So spec+APC coexistence for hybrids existed and regressed somewhere between v0.24.0 and the current nightly.

Repro (nightly):

```bash
docker run --rm --init --network host --gpus all --ipc host \
  -v /opt/models:/models -e CUTE_DSL_ARCH=sm_121a \
  vllm/vllm-openai:nightly /models/qwen3.8-27b-nvfp4 \
  --served-model-name bench --port 10099 \
  --max-model-len 65536 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.30 \
  --max-num-seqs 1 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}'
# send any >3,300-token prompt twice; watch vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total stay 0
# drop --speculative-config and the second send hits ~all full blocks
```

Possibly related but distinct: #53670 (hits occur but recompute per hit), #41884 (DFlash+APC IndexError crash — we see silent zero-hit, not a crash), #26201 (tracking).

Is the suppression intentional (spec-decode + hybrid APC support not yet wired on the new path), or a regression? If intentional, a startup warning like the align-mode one would save users from silently losing their cache. Happy to run further diagnostics on this hardware.

items.title: [Bug][ROCm] GLM-5.3-Flash kpool indexer overwrites its own KV cache: backend advertises a kernel block size the kernels do not use
items.body:
### Summary

On ROCm, the GLM-5.3-Flash kpool sparse indexer **silently overwrites its own KV cache**. 4096 pool entries are written into 864 distinct slots, so ~79 % of the indexer's keys are wrong. The model still produces fluent text, so nothing crashes — long-context recall just degrades, and `temperature=0` stops being reproducible because the damage depends on which physical blocks the allocator hands out.

This is **ROCm-only** and distinct from #40018 (whose fix, #43781, is present in the tree I tested).

### Root cause

`DeepseekV32IndexerBackend.get_supported_kernel_block_sizes()` (`vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/indexer.py`):

```python
return [1, MultipleOf(16)] if current_platform.is_rocm() else [64]
```

On CUDA the backend declares exactly `[64]`, so vLLM sets `kernel_block_size = 64`, `BlockTable.use_hybrid_blocks = True`, and builds a kernel-granular block table. On ROCm it declares "any multiple of 16", so the hybrid aligner's choice (640 tokens here) is taken as natively supported: `blocks_per_kv_block == 1`, **no kernel-granular block table**.

But the kernels do not read 640-token blocks. DeepGEMM/AITER paged-MQA reads pool pages of 32 states; with `tokens_per_state == index_kpool == 4` that is 128 tokens. So the storage block (640 tok = 160 states) is five pages, and both `slot_mapping` and `cp_gather_indexer_k_quant_cache_triton` address it with the **page** size (32) while the block table holds **spec-block** ids — a 5x over-subscription.

The intended split is even documented in `vllm/models/glm5next/nvidia/attention.py` as `storage_kernel_block_size`, but that identifier appears nowhere else in the tree — it was never implemented.

### Evidence (8x MI350X, gfx950, TP8, ROCm 7.2.3, `index_kpool=4`, `block_size=640`)

Instrumented at the indexer, two identical requests, prefix caching off:

| | before | after fix |
|---|---|---|
| distinct cache slots written (of 4096 pools) | **864** | **4096** |
| `max_slot` | 863 (= 26x32+31) | 4159 (= 26x160+…) |
| distinct gathered K rows (of 4000) | **864** | **4000** |
| rows duplicated at period 256 | 3488 | **0** |
| block-table entries used | 27/125, **99 zeros** | 125/125, 0 zeros |
| block-table width | 205 | 1025 (= 205x5) |

Zero entries are not skipped: the gather clamps an invalid block to `safe_block_id = 0` and reads physical block 0 repeatedly.

Layer-by-layer hashing of two identical requests shows the divergence starting exactly at layer 3, the first `deepseek_sparse_attention` layer, while `q`, `gate_score`, `ape` and the pre-pool `k` are bit-identical — only the gathered `k_quant` differs.

### Reproducer

Needle-in-a-haystack, needle at 50 %, `temperature=0`, ~40k tokens:

```
before:  3/3 missed   (model never finds the key)
after:   3/3 found
```

Sweep on the fixed build (tuned config, compiled, prefix caching on):

| prompt tokens | needle |
|---|---|
| 6 687 | found |
| 27 141 | found |
| 54 265 | found |
| 110 561 | found |

### Fix

Let the indexer cache advertise the kernel block size its kernels actually use, so vLLM's existing `use_hybrid_blocks` machinery builds the kernel-granular block table:

```python
# vllm/models/glm5next/nvidia/attention.py
class Glm5NextIndexerCache(DeepseekV32IndexerCache):
    def get_attn_backend(self):
        # DeepGEMM paged-MQA reads pool pages of 32 or 64 states; with
        # tokens_per_state == index_kpool that is 32*kpool / 64*kpool tokens.
        return _kpool_indexer_backend(self._index_kpool)   # -> [32*kpool, 64*kpool]
```

Allocation is unchanged (`block_size` stays 640, uniform page size preserved) — only the addressing is corrected, so there is no extra memory and no throughput cost.

The general form of the bug is that `get_supported_kernel_block_sizes()` is declared in **tokens** while the constraint is in **states**; any spec with `tokens_per_state > 1` needs the declaration scaled by it. The ROCm `MultipleOf(16)` branch is what lets the mismatch through.

Happy to send this as a PR if the approach looks right — in particular whether you would prefer fixing the ROCm branch of `DeepseekV32IndexerBackend` directly (it would need access to `tokens_per_state`) over a GLM-specific backend.

items.title: [Feature]: cannot budget KV cache per GPU when one card of a DP group is shared with another process
items.body:
## TL;DR

- One model served with `--data-parallel-size 3` across 3 GPUs; a second, much smaller vLLM server shares GPU 0 with it.
- The budget vLLM sizes from is a fraction of the **whole** card and **one value for every rank**, so the shared card caps the group: GPU 1 and 2 hold ~17 GiB each that nothing can use, while GPU 0 is left at ~0.15 GiB free and dies with `torch.OutOfMemoryError` under load.
- CUDA graph memory is not reserved either (#49224), which puts every rank ~2.3 GiB past its own budget on top of that.

**Takeaway:** it would be good to have a way to state, per GPU / per rank, how much memory a worker may use.

> Drafted with an LLM from my own investigation notes. Every figure below comes from my startup logs and `nvidia-smi`; the source references were checked against the shipped image.

## Setup

3x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (94.97 GiB usable each), NixOS, Docker, image `vllm/vllm-openai:qwen38-flash-next` (vLLM `0.1.dev20073+g8e685d198`).

Two containers on one host. **A** — the chat model, sees all 3 GPUs (abridged):

```
vllm serve unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 \
  --data-parallel-size 3 --enable-expert-parallel \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.821 \
  --max-model-len 256000 --max-num-batched-tokens 24000 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}'
```

**B** — an embedding server, pinned to GPU 0: `vllm serve unsloth/Qwen3-Embedding-8B --runner pooling --max-model-len 8192`.

B is already resident when A starts, so GPU 0 has ~12 GiB less free than GPU 1 and GPU 2.

## Problem

Each rank's own startup advisory (`gpu_worker.py:919`), abridged:

| rank | free at startup | weights+non-torch | peak act | CUDA graphs* | KV allocated | "to fully utilize gpu memory" |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DP0 (GPU 0, shared) | 82.45 | 60.00 | 2.85 | 2.18 | 15.13 | **17.29** |
| DP1 (GPU 1) | 93.98 | 59.87 | 2.85 | 2.18 | 15.26 | **28.93** |
| DP2 (GPU 2) | 93.98 | 59.59 | 2.85 | 2.18 | 15.54 | **29.21** |

GiB. *the graph figure is vLLM's own, measured after KV was already sized.

Three distinct things:

1. `--gpu-memory-utilization` is a fraction of the **total** memory of the card, not of what is free on it. On GPU 0 another container holds ~12 GiB, so the same fraction promises more there than exists.
2. That value is applied to **every** DP rank, so the shared card sets the ceiling for the whole group and the other two cards keep ~17 GiB each that nothing can use. The right-hand column is the per-card figure vLLM itself computes (`kv_cache_memory_bytes_to_gpu_limit`) and then only logs.
3. CUDA graph memory is not reserved: `Using V2 Model Runner`, whose `profile_cudagraph_memory()` returns 0 (#49224). The advisory above confirms it — `77.98 - 60.00 - 2.85 = 15.13`, exactly the KV allocated, graphs charged afterwards — so every rank sits ~2.3 GiB past its own budget.

GPU 0 therefore runs at ~0.15 GiB free. Under traffic a 470-786 MiB activation inside a prefill kernel fails, `torch.OutOfMemoryError`, engine down. It presents as an intermittent, unrelated-looking crash.

## What I have tried

- Lowering `--gpu-memory-utilization`: stops the crash, but it is still uniform, so the unshared cards lose exactly the same amount.
- `--kv-cache-memory-bytes`: absolute and stable, but still one value for all ranks, so it must be sized for the shared card; it also bypasses the profiler, so an over-estimate fails at boot instead of degrading.
- Starting B before A so A's startup guard observes B's footprint: necessary, but it does not change the uniform sizing.
- `VLLM_ENABLE_STARTUP_PLAN=1`: persists values per rank, but stores the request-bounded figure, not the per-card one.

## What would help

It would be good to have a way to state how much memory a worker may use that is not "a fraction of the whole device, identical on every DP rank" — for instance an absolute per-GPU budget, or per-rank KV sizing from the free memory each worker already measures.

## Related

- #49224 — CUDA graph memory not reserved by the V2 runner.
- #40937 — memory budget describing the whole device rather than what the process may use (HAMi/MIG/MPS).

items.title: [Bug]: [XPU] moe_wna16 AWQ fallback compares CUDA device_capability, always -1 on XPU
items.body:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

- vLLM version: `0.21.1.dev18+g8df6feb7d` (`intel/vllm:0.21.0-xpu` Docker image)
- Platform: `device_config=xpu`
- Hardware: Intel Arc Pro B60 (Battlemage, BMG)
- OS: Windows 11 + WSL2, Docker Desktop backend
- Model: `QuantTrio/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-AWQ` — native AWQ format, MoE (`Qwen3MoeForCausalLM`)

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Follow-up to #54349 (which routes AWQ MoE layers on XPU away from the CUDA-only Marlin kernel into the `moe_wna16` Triton fallback). That fallback has its own, separate CUDA-only gate — twice in the same file — that rejects XPU unconditionally, because `current_platform.get_device_capability()` returns `None` on XPU (a CUDA SM-version concept that doesn't apply):

```python
# vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/moe_wna16.py
capability_tuple = current_platform.get_device_capability()
device_capability = (
    -1 if capability_tuple is None else capability_tuple.to_int()
)
awq_min_capability = AutoAWQConfig.get_min_capability()
if device_capability < awq_min_capability:
    raise ValueError(...)
```

and the equivalent check in `is_moe_wna16_compatible()`. `device_capability` is always `-1` on XPU, so both checks always fail once XPU is (correctly) routed here.

### Error

```
ValueError: The quantization method moe_wna16 + awq is not supported for the current GPU. Minimum capability: 75. Current capability: -1.
```

### Suggested fix

Bypass both occurrences for XPU:

```diff
-            if device_capability < awq_min_capability:
+            if not current_platform.is_xpu() and device_capability < awq_min_capability:
```
```diff
         awq_compatible = (
             quant_method == "awq"
             and num_bits == 4
-            and device_capability >= awq_min_capability
+            and (device_capability >= awq_min_capability or current_platform.is_xpu())
         )
```

### Verification of the fix

The actual compute path this method dispatches to (`fused_experts`) has no CUDA-specific code in this file — it's a generic dispatch, so the capability check reads as an overly conservative CUDA-era gate rather than a real hardware limitation. Applied both patches locally on top of #54349's fix (against the `0.21.0-xpu` image's version of the file — confirmed the identical checks are still present, unchanged, on current `main`). With both patches, `QuantTrio/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-AWQ` loads successfully end-to-end on an Arc Pro B60 (all 48 MoE layers, all safetensors shards) and serves correct, coherent completions and tool calls via the OpenAI-compatible API.

items.title: [Bug]: [XPU] AWQ MoE selector (check_moe_marlin_supports_config) ignores XPU platform, crashes on Marlin path
items.body:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

- vLLM version: `0.21.1.dev18+g8df6feb7d` (`intel/vllm:0.21.0-xpu` Docker image)
- Platform: `device_config=xpu`
- Hardware: Intel Arc Pro B60 (Battlemage, BMG)
- OS: Windows 11 + WSL2, Docker Desktop backend
- Model: `QuantTrio/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-AWQ` — native AWQ format (`quant_method: "awq"`, 4-bit, group_size=128), a MoE model (`Qwen3MoeForCausalLM`)

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On XPU, loading a native-AWQ-format MoE model routes `FusedMoE` layers into the CUDA-only Marlin kernel and crashes, because the platform-bypass check only excludes ROCm:

```python
# vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/marlin_utils.py
def check_moe_marlin_supports_config(config, group_size, allow_tile_padding=False):
    if current_platform.is_rocm():
        return False
    ...
```

This is the same shape of bug already reported and confirmed in #43750 for the **compressed-tensors** format selector — this issue is the equivalent gap in the **native AWQ** format selector (`awq.py`'s `get_quant_method`, which also calls this same helper), a different code path, so filing separately rather than as a duplicate.

### Reproduction

```bash
vllm serve QuantTrio/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-AWQ \
  --quantization awq --dtype float16 \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --max-model-len 32768
```

### Error

```
ValueError: Marlin does not support weight_bits = uint4. Only types = [] are supported (for group_size = 128, device_capability = -1, zp = True).
```

`device_capability = -1` because `current_platform.get_device_capability()` returns `None` on XPU (a CUDA SM-version concept that doesn't apply) — the Marlin support table has no valid entry for that, so it always fails once routed there.

### Suggested fix

Add `is_xpu()` to the platform bypass, matching the existing ROCm treatment:

```diff
 def check_moe_marlin_supports_config(config, group_size, allow_tile_padding=False):
-    if current_platform.is_rocm():
+    if current_platform.is_rocm() or current_platform.is_xpu():
         return False
```

### Verification of the fix

Applied this change locally (against the `0.21.0-xpu` image's version of the file, `check_moe_marlin_supports_layer` — the function has since been refactored into `check_moe_marlin_supports_config` on `main`, confirmed the same missing check is still present there). With the fix applied, layers correctly fall through to the Triton-based `MoeWNA16` method instead (logged as `Layer '...' is not supported by AWQMoeMarlin. Falling back to Moe WNA16 kernels.`) — which itself hits a second, related bug in `moe_wna16.py`'s own AWQ-compatibility gate (filed separately, since it's a distinct file/function): #54350

items.title: [Bug]: Assistant `content=null` + `tool_calls` renders literal "None" into chat template context — degenerate outputs in agent workloads
items.body:
### Environment
- vLLM: `v0.1.dev20051+g487ecf187` (also present on recent mainline `dev` builds)
- Model: GLM-5.3-Flash (any GLM chat template that emits per-turn `<think>` and renders `{{ content }}` for assistant turns; the keys/GLM stock `chat_template.jinja` is affected)
- Hardware: 4× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120), TP4
- Client: pi agent (any agent harness sending `content: null` + `tool_calls` assistant turns — standard OpenAI agent format; cursor/openai-python do the same)

### Symptom
Long agent sessions (multi-turn tool calling) intermittently produce **degenerate repetitive outputs** (e.g. an infinite loop of `# --` or a single reasoning loop consuming the entire `max_tokens` budget with zero content tokens). Probability increases with the number of tool-call turns in history.

### Root cause
When an agent client sends an assistant message with `content: null` and `tool_calls`, the message passes through to `apply_chat_template` with `content=None`. The GLM chat template renders this turn as:

```
<|assistant|><think></think>None<tool_call>bash<arg_key>...
                       ^^^^ literal "None"
```

Verified with `tokenizer.apply_chat_template` (transformers 4.5x):

```python
msgs = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "check metrics"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": None, "tool_calls": [...]},   # agent turn
    {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "c0", "content": "run=3"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "continue"},
]
tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tools=tools, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
# → '<|assistant|><think></think>None<tool_call>bash...'
#    with content="" instead of None:
# → '<|assistant|><think></think><tool_call>bash...'   (clean)
```

Every tool-calling turn injects one literal `None` token-sequence into the context. After 8-20 turns (a normal agent session) the model's in-context pattern degrades and reasoning collapses into repetition loops.

### Degeneration repro (against a live server)
8-turn tool-call history + code-generation request, `temperature=0.2`:

| | before fix | after fix |
|---|---|---|
| reasoning 8-gram repetition rate | **1.000** (pure loop, 2721 chars) | **0.000** (1425 chars, coherent) |
| content tokens produced | 0 (budget eaten by the loop) | normal |
| finish | length | tool_calls / stop |

### Proposed fix (minimal, protocol-layer)
Normalize in `_postprocess_messages` (`vllm/entrypoints/chat_utils.py`) — this function already normalizes `tool_calls[].function.arguments` for the same class of problem:

```python
def _postprocess_messages(messages: list[ConversationMessage]) -> None:
    # Agent clients (pi/cursor/openai sdk) send assistant messages with
    # content:null + tool_calls. Templates that render {{ content }} emit a
    # literal "None" into the context; over many agent turns this degrades
    # generation into repetition loops. Normalize to "".
    for message in messages:
        if (
            message.get("role") == "assistant"
            and message.get("content") is None
            and "tool_calls" in message
        ):
            message["content"] = ""
    ...  # existing arguments-dict normalization
```

Verified on our deployment: same request that looped at 1.000 repetition now returns a clean, working tool call (`finish_reason=tool_calls`).

### Impact
Any model whose chat template renders assistant `content` unconditionally (GLM family at minimum; likely others) + any agent-format client. This is silent: outputs look like "model quality problems", not template bugs — worth a regression test in the chat-template suite (assistant content=None + tool_calls round-trip).
